candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest predicts MALWARE with probability 0.925, and all 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking. However, each SHAP contribution is small (+0.0045 to +0.0100), and most n-gram frequencies are extremely low (about 0.000005 to 0.000191). The highest-frequency items are LEA MOVDQA (0.001604) and DEC DEC (0.001104). The top-ranked n-grams (SUB CMOVG, ADC SUB, LEA ADC, SETG ADD, SETC AND, SETNC MOVZX) point to carry-propagating, multi-precision-style integer arithmetic with flag-based branchless selection. That is consistent with hashing or big-number computation, but it also appears in ordinary math or runtime code. The SIMD patterns (PCMPEQB PMOVMSKB, PCMPESTRI CMP, VPCMPEQB VPAND, MOVDQU MOVDQA, LEA MOVDQA) are typical of vectorized byte comparison and memory block handling. They are common in optimized string and memory routines and are not specific to mining. CPUID CMP indicates CPU feature detection, which miners often perform to choose an optimized code path, but legitimate software does the same. MOVAPD DIVSD and MOVSD ADDSD are scalar floating-point operations with no obvious link to mining. BSF MOV, DEC BTS, XOR NOP, ADD OR and AND MOVQ are generic bit-manipulation or padding sequences. The evidence contains no function-level context and no mining-specific signature, such as a dense cluster of rotate/shift/XOR round-function patterns or AES-instruction sequences. The model's score is high, but the supporting n-grams are individually weak and ambiguous. The evidence is suggestive of arithmetic-heavy, CPU-optimized code but is inconclusive for cryptojacking.

evidence_analysis.assessment: Branchless conditional selection after subtraction. Seen in constant-time or multi-precision arithmetic, but also in compiler-optimized min/max logic. Top contributor, but not specific to mining.
Add-with-carry followed by subtract suggests multi-word arithmetic (big-integer style), which is relevant to hashing and crypto math. Also common in generic bignum or 64-bit-on-32-bit arithmetic.
Masking followed by a 64-bit SIMD/GPR move. Generic data manipulation with weak cryptojacking specificity.
Address computation feeding a carry-add, consistent with multi-precision arithmetic loops. Moderately suggestive but ambiguous.
Flag-to-register materialization followed by accumulation. A branchless comparison idiom, common in compiled code.
Carry-flag capture and masking, again pointing to carry-chain arithmetic. Consistent with crypto-style math but not conclusive.
SSE4.2 explicit-length string comparison. Typically used for optimized string search or parsing, with no direct mining link.
Classic SIMD byte-compare and mask-extract idiom for strlen/memchr-style routines. Common in benign runtime libraries.
AVX-based byte comparison and masking. Shows the binary uses AVX-optimized code paths, which are common in both benign and miner code.
Address calculation followed by aligned 128-bit load/store. This is the most frequent n-gram (0.001604) and indicates vectorized memory handling that is typical of optimized library code.
Floating-point division on SSE registers. Not characteristic of integer-heavy hashing, so weakly relevant.
CPU feature detection followed by comparison. Miners use this for dispatching optimized implementations, but many legitimate programs and runtimes do too.
Unaligned-to-aligned 128-bit data movement, typical of block copy or buffer handling in optimized code.
Repeated decrements, likely loop counters or unrolled loop bookkeeping. Fairly frequent (0.001104) but generic.
Bit-scan used in bit manipulation, string scanning or normalization. Often follows PMOVMSKB in string routines, so likely benign runtime code.
Carry-flag materialization with zero-extension, again indicating carry-aware arithmetic. Weakly supportive.
Scalar double-precision load and add, suggesting ordinary floating-point computation with no specific mining relevance.
Register zeroing or XOR followed by alignment padding. A compiler artifact with little diagnostic value.
Generic arithmetic and bitwise combination. Slightly more frequent (0.000191) but non-specific.
Decrement followed by bit-test-and-set. An uncommon bit-manipulation pairing, but with a very low count and no clear mining semantics.
